clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic mutations in TFG, the TRK-fused gene.
Characteristic triad of early-onset spastic paraplegia, optic atrophy with reduced visual acuity, and a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy that is often demyelinating or mixed.
Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood with delayed motor milestones and progressive lower-limb spasticity.
The coexistence of central pyramidal signs with peripheral nerve involvement is a key clue - a spastic paraplegia plus neuropathy plus optic atrophy pattern.
Distal wasting, pes cavus or other foot deformity and contractures may develop from the neuropathic component.

TFG encodes an endoplasmic reticulum exit-site protein, and allelic disorders include autosomal dominant hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy proximal type and Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2, so the phenotype depends on the specific variant and zygosity.
Visual evoked potentials and nerve conduction studies substantiate the multi-system picture.
First delineated in a consanguineous family; consider SPG57 in early-onset HSP accompanied by visual failure and neuropathy.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG57 results from biallelic mutation of TFG, which encodes the TRK-fused gene protein. TFG oligomerises at endoplasmic reticulum exit sites, where it organises COPII coat assembly and the anterograde ER-to-Golgi secretory pathway. The recessive HSP-associated substitution impairs TFG self-assembly and protein export from the ER, with secondary disturbance of proteostasis and axonal transport. Because long central motor axons, optic nerve fibres and peripheral nerves are all heavily dependent on efficient secretory trafficking, their degeneration produces the composite phenotype of spastic paraplegia, optic atrophy and peripheral neuropathy that distinguishes this subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Complicated recessive HSPs with thin corpus callosum or neuropathy: SPG11 (spatacsin), SPG15 (ZFYVE26), SPG7 (paraplegin)
Other complicated recessive subtypes: SPG35 (FA2H), SPG54 (DDHD2), SPG5 (CYP7B1)
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies or Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease accompanied by pyramidal signs
Autosomal recessive optic atrophy syndromes and mitochondrial optic neuropathies such as Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
Friedreich ataxia and other spinocerebellar disorders with optic and peripheral involvement
Metabolic leukodystrophies such as metachromatic leukodystrophy causing combined central and peripheral demyelination
additionalInvestigations: TFG sequencing within hereditary spastic paraplegia and neuropathy gene panels, or exome sequencing
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to characterise the neuropathy as demyelinating or axonal
MRI of the brain and spine, with attention to the optic nerves
Ophthalmology review with optical coherence tomography and visual evoked potentials to confirm optic atrophy
Somatosensory and motor evoked potentials to assess central conduction
Exclusion bloods including vitamin B12, copper and very-long-chain fatty acids, plus a metabolic and leukodystrophy screen
Genetic counselling and testing of relatives given the recessive inheritance
redFlags: Rapidly worsening vision or a new central scotoma requiring urgent ophthalmological assessment
Sudden or asymmetric progression suggesting an acquired inflammatory or compressive process
Prominent bulbar, respiratory or autonomic involvement
Systemic or metabolic decompensation pointing to a leukodystrophy or mitochondrial disorder
reference.prognosis: SPG57 is progressive, combining worsening spasticity, visual loss and neuropathic disability, so that ambulation and vision decline through childhood and adolescence; the rate varies between individuals and supportive management helps preserve function.
pitfalls: Attributing the picture to an isolated neuropathy or to isolated optic atrophy and missing the unifying diagnosis
Forgetting that TFG variants cause several distinct disorders, including proximal hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2, depending on variant and inheritance
Overlooking the peripheral neuropathy because upper motor neurone signs dominate the examination
Mistaking the combined central and peripheral demyelination for a primary leukodystrophy without genetic confirmation
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for combined spasticity and neuropathic distal weakness, with orthoses and adaptive aids
Ophthalmological review and low-vision support for optic atrophy
Orthopaedic and orthotic management of pes cavus, foot deformity and contractures arising from the neuropathy
Neuropathic pain management where present, with surveillance of the peripheral neuropathy
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with carrier testing of relatives
Multidisciplinary neurology, ophthalmology, rehabilitation and orthopaedic input
